summary: This informational document analyzes threats to Multipath TCP (MPTCP) that remain after the protocol's earlier security work, and explores possible solutions to address them.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipath TCP lets one connection use several network paths at once, which means a running connection can be given new addresses as the device moves. RFC 7430 looks at what an attacker can do with that, and finds five attacks: one where an attacker who is nowhere near the connection can take it over, two where a flood of handshake messages stops new paths being opened, and two where someone watching the connection can interfere. It ends with a recommended fix for the first of them.

questions: what is the mptcp add_addr attack
how to prevent mptcp syn flooding
what are the residual threats for mptcp
subtitle: The attacks that Multipath TCP still leaves open, and the changes that would close them.

tldr.problem: Multipath TCP was designed so that adding a second address to a running connection could not make it less secure than an ordinary connection. That design left several attacks open, including one that lets an off-path attacker take over a session.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7430 works through five attacks: an address announcement hijack, two denial of service attacks against the handshake that opens extra paths, and two attacks that need an eavesdropper on the path. For each it states what the attacker needs to know and what would prevent it.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends that the address announcement carry a message authentication code over the address and the key, which would bring it to the same level as the handshake message it already protects, and notes that the remaining eavesdropping problems are fundamental to supporting network address translation.

today: RFC 7430 is an Informational RFC published in July 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It analyses the Multipath TCP specification as it stood then and recommends a change to it; the document does not say whether that change was made.

sections.title: Why a Second Threat Analysis
sections.content:
The document complements the threat analysis for Multipath TCP given in RFC 6181, which covered the general solution space of extending TCP to work with several addresses per connection. That analysis was written before the Multipath TCP specification itself was finished, and it drew on the experience of other multi-address protocols, notably Shim6, SCTP and Mobile IPv6. This document takes the mechanisms as specified in RFC 6824 and analyses them for vulnerabilities, with the aim of identifying security issues and proposing enhancements.

The goal of the security mechanisms in the Multipath TCP specification was to make the protocol no worse than the single-path TCP already available, and the document takes that as its yardstick. It therefore covers only the threats that are specific to Multipath TCP as defined in RFC 6824, which cannot happen with single-path TCP. Threats common to both are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: An earlier document analysed the general idea of giving a connection more than one address, before the protocol itself existed. This one takes the protocol as written and looks for holes in it, using the same test the designers used: the protocol must not be weaker than ordinary TCP.

sections.title: The Kinds of Attacker
sections.content:
Attackers are classified first by where they are. An off-path attacker never needs to be on any of the paths of the session at any point in its life, and so cannot eavesdrop any of its packets. A partial-time on-path attacker needs to be on at least one of the paths during part of the session's life, but not all of it, and can be in the forward direction, the backward direction, or both, for the initial subflow or for other subflows. An on-path attacker must be on at least one of the paths for the whole duration of the session, again in either direction and for any subflow.

Attackers are also classified by what they do. An eavesdropper can capture packets of the session but cannot change, discard or delay any of them. An active attacker can change, discard or delay packets. The document considers five combinations: an on-path eavesdropper, an on-path active attacker, an off-path active attacker, a partial-time on-path eavesdropper and a partial-time on-path active attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts attackers two ways. By position: never on the path, on it for part of the time, or on it throughout. By what they do: only watching, or also able to change and drop packets. Each attack that follows is then labelled with the kind of attacker it needs.

sections.title: The ADD_ADDR Hijack
sections.content:
The first attack uses the option that announces an alternative address for a connection, and it needs an off-path active attacker. Host A, with address IPA, has a Multipath TCP session with Host B, with address IPB, using ports PA and PB and session tokens TA and TB. The attacker, Host C, owns address IPC and forges a packet from IPA to IPB with the acknowledgement flag set, a valid sequence number and a valid acknowledgement number, carrying an ADD_ADDR option that announces IPC as an alternative address. The option also carries an 8-bit address identifier, which gives no strong security benefit.

Host B replies with a SYN carrying the join option, the token TA and a fresh random nonce RB. The attacker rewrites it so that it appears to come from IPC to IPA, and Host A answers with a SYN and acknowledgement carrying a valid message authentication code computed with the session key. The attacker rewrites that to appear to come from IPC to IPB, Host B verifies the code and replies with the final acknowledgement carrying its own valid code, and the attacker rewrites that once more, to IPA. Host A then creates the new subflow, and the attacker is in the middle of it. The original subflow still runs, so to take the whole session over the attacker sends two reset messages, one to each host, forged from the other host's address and with a valid sequence number.

To do this the attacker needs the four values that identify the connection, a valid sequence number, a valid acknowledgement number and an address identifier that is not already in use. The addresses can be assumed known, the server port is known if the attacker knows the application, and only the client port must be guessed, which depends on the size of the ephemeral port range and on whether the client randomises its ports. A valid sequence number must be guessed blindly, and the chances depend on the size of the target's receive window, which automatic buffer tuning can make very large, up to 2 MB. The acknowledgement number is only loosely checked unless the implementation follows the stricter rule of RFC 5961. The address identifier only has to differ from the ones already in use, so a random value will do.

The document notes that the attack requires forged source addresses, so it cannot be carried out where ingress filtering or source address validation is deployed, but that ingress filtering is not deployed as widely as one would hope and cannot be relied on. It gives two expressions for the number of packets an attacker must send: one for implementations without the stricter checks, which depends on the receive window, the ephemeral port range and the segment size, and one for implementations with them, which adds a factor for the largest send window ever used. With a 16 KB window and 4000 ephemeral ports, the first expression gives 699050 packets; with a 2 MB window it gives 5461. The second expression, with the stricter checks and all values equal, gives 45812984490 packets for the same 16 KB window and 4000 ports, and 2796202 for a 2 MB window.
sections.plainLanguage: An address announcement inside a running connection carries no proof of who sent it. An attacker who is nowhere near the connection can send one with a forged address, and if the receiving end opens a new path towards the announced address, the attacker ends up sitting in the middle of that path. The attacker has to guess a port number and a sequence number, so the attack takes many attempts, but the document calculates that with a large receive window it can take only a few thousand packets.

sections.title: Denial of Service Against New Paths
sections.content:
The second attack is a denial of service against the handshake that opens an extra path, and it needs an off-path active attacker. As specified, the opening message of that handshake creates state on the host that receives it, because the message carries the 32-bit token that identifies the session and the 32-bit random nonce used in the authentication code, and neither is repeated in the third packet of the handshake. An attacker that sends such a message with the valid token TB to Host B therefore makes Host B create state. The number of half-open connections a host keeps per session is limited and is implementation dependent, and the attacker exhausts that limit by sending the message with different five-tuples. The forged source address will usually be one that is not in use, because otherwise the reply from Host B would draw a reset from the impersonated node and clear the state. This prevents Host A from opening any further paths to Host B.

The attacker needs the token, which it can obtain as a partial-time on-path eavesdropper watching a path being opened, or by guessing the 32-bit value. The proposed fix is to extend the third packet of the handshake to carry the token and the random nonce that were sent in the opening message, and to have Host B generate its own nonce reproducibly, for example as a hash of the five-tuple, the initial sequence number and a local secret. Host B could then answer the opening message without creating any state, and only create it when the third packet arrives and the authentication code can be checked.

The third attack uses the same messages to amplify a SYN flood. SYN flooding exhausts a server's resources with SYN messages, and the usual answer is SYN cookies, which let the server process the first message without keeping state. Multipath TCP can process the first SYN that way, but the opening message of an extra path cannot, because it carries the token and the nonce. So an attacker can open a session with one ordinary SYN and then send as many opening messages as the server supports, each with a different source address and port, consuming server state at the cost of one state record on the attacker's own side. The fix for the previous attack also stops this one, and limiting the number of half-open paths to a low number, for example three, would limit its impact as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening an extra path needs a message that carries the session token, and that message makes the receiving host store something before it knows whether the sender is genuine. An attacker can therefore fill up the host's allowance of pending connections and stop the real client opening any more paths. The same gap lets an attacker multiply the cost of a SYN flood, because the protection that lets a server handle floods without storing state does not apply to these messages.

sections.title: Eavesdroppers and Address Substitution
sections.content:
The fourth attack needs a partial-time on-path eavesdropper. An attacker that is present when the initial handshake takes place learns the keys used in the session, which lets it leave the path and still hijack the session later. This weakness was identified when the Multipath TCP security solution was designed, and the threat was accepted at the time.

The document enumerates the ways to prevent it, each with its own trade-offs: hash chains, which have been explored for Multipath TCP; the use of the keys from a Secure Socket Layer connection; cryptographically generated addresses, which have been used to secure other multi-addressed protocols such as Shim6; tcpcrypt; and DNSSEC, which has been proposed to secure Mobile IP.

The fifth attack also needs a partial-time on-path eavesdropper, and it exploits the same message that opens an extra path. An attacker on the path can replace the source address in that message with any address it chooses. This weakness too was identified earlier and accepted. The document calls it fundamental, because Multipath TCP has to work through network address translators to be deployable on the Internet, and what a translator does is indistinguishable from this attack. The source address therefore cannot be secured, since securing it would stop the protocol working through a translator, and the solution cannot rely on securing the address. A more promising approach is to secure the payload exchanged instead, which limits what the attack can achieve.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attacks need someone to be listening on the path. One learns the session keys during the handshake and can come back later to take the session over. The other replaces the address in the message that opens an extra path. The second cannot be fixed by protecting the address, because a network address translator looks exactly like the attack, and Multipath TCP has to work with translators to be usable at all. The document therefore points at protecting the data instead.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The Multipath TCP specification is Experimental and there is an effort to move it to the Standards Track. The document recommends two threads of work: improving Multipath TCP security so the specification can become a Standards Track document, and separately analysing further enhancements for a more secure version of the protocol.

For the first thread, the view is that the address announcement attack must be addressed, and that the fix should be to include a message authentication code in the announcement, using the address being added as input to the code along with the key. That would make the announcement as secure as the join message, and a better way of creating the session key would then improve both, since both use the same key. The document argues that this is enough for Standards Track, because the resulting security level is similar to that of single-path TCP and is exactly the level already reached by SCTP with dynamic addresses, a Standards Track document that requires an authentication mechanism for the same reason.

For the second thread, the document repeats its earlier conclusion that securing the join messages is fundamentally incompatible with network address translation, so a solution is likely to involve protecting the data itself. It points to tcpcrypt and to integration with SSL as promising directions.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommended fix for the session hijack is to sign the address announcement with the session key, so that an attacker cannot invent an address without the key. That brings Multipath TCP to the same level of protection as SCTP when addresses are added to a connection. The document also notes that the problems which need an eavesdropper cannot be fixed at the address level, so the remaining work is about protecting the data.
